executive_assessment.text: Isfara village evidence distinguishes perceived scarcity from measured runoff, with historical allocation and institutional constraints rather than a simple drought-causes-conflict account.
Ak-Bashat and Kashka-Suu provide named local cases; FAO-reported sensor and storage benefits are not independently proven effects.

geographic_notes.text: The Isfara supplies irrigation and city water to more than 40 villages in Batken district and downstream Isfara district in Tajikistan.
In the 2019 six-village Isfara study, 72% perceived lower winter snowfall and 78% hotter summers; separate snow and upstream precipitation measurements were incomplete.

The 2019 Isfara study records perceived irrigation shortages and lower yields associated with erosion, pests and disease; perceived falling river water contrasted with an increasing measured runoff trend.
FAO's May 2024 feature links stream drying in Ak-Bashat to climate change; one farmer describes switching from orchards to cattle and water depletion causing disputes.
FAO's May 2024 feature reports canal sensors in Naryn and Batken pilot areas supporting water accounting and rational allocation, and claims irrigation disputes were eliminated.
FAO's May 2024 feature describes community construction of a Kashka-Suu artificial glacier for seasonal water, with additional locally funded structures; benefits were not independently evaluated.

At February 2023 consultations, representatives of Batken, Osh and Jalal-Abad described water shortages, drought, forest fires, heat illness and limited finance; the release is not a completed risk assessment.
UNDP's February 2024 release describes adaptation-plan development as a next step after February 2023 provincial consultations; later plan status is unverified.

known_gaps.text: Automated machine-screening is not independent source verification. Routine/default app-use approval does not certify claims or sources. 19 of 20 evidence records and 2 of 2 pathways lack claim-level verification in this remediation; review the linked records before relying on them.
The 2021 NDC explicitly warns that inequitable access to resources amid climate pressures can lead to social conflict; this is a potential risk statement, not observed conflict attribution.
The 2025 CCDR and NDC 3.0 full PDFs were too large for browser retrieval, and the Climate Risk Profile was blocked; projections here are taken only from the opened CCDR summary.

The strongest local climate-conflict evidence concerns Batken-Sughd and dates mainly from 2019-2021; these records should not be read as a 2026 update.
The FAO technology and artificial-glacier claims are implementer-reported and lack independent outcome evaluation in the inspected source.
No separate current primary study was accessed on conflict-driven exclusion from climate adaptation beyond shared-water infrastructure and governance constraints.
The 2019-2021 cross-border evidence is historical. No claim is made that those border arrangements or conflict conditions remain current.
